title: Definition of Data Structure & Data Types
badge: KTU Part A • 3 Marks • Bloom's K1
points: Data Type: A collection of values and a set of operations allowed on those values (e.g., int, float, char).
Data Structure: A specialized format for organizing, processing, retrieving, and storing data in computer memory efficiently.
Linear vs Non-Linear: Linear (Array, Stack, Queue, Linked List) where elements are sequential; Non-Linear (Tree, Graph) hierarchical.
Classification: Primitive (built-in) vs Non-Primitive (user-defined derived structures).
exam_tip: In Part A, define both Data Type and Data Structure to get 1.5 + 1.5 = 3 Marks.

title: Abstract Data Types (ADT)
badge: KTU Part A • 3 Marks • Bloom's K2
points: Definition: A mathematical model for data types where a data type is defined by its behavior (semantics) from user point of view.
Encapsulation: Separates public interface specifications from private implementation details.
Axiomatic Specification: Operations are specified by preconditions (requirements) and postconditions (results).
Classic Examples: Stack ADT (LIFO), Queue ADT (FIFO), List ADT, Priority Queue ADT.
exam_tip: Mention that ADT specifies WHAT operations are performed, not HOW they are implemented.

title: Time Complexity vs Space Complexity
badge: KTU Part A • 3 Marks • Bloom's K2
points: Time Complexity: Quantification of computer CPU execution time required by an algorithm as a function of input size n.
Space Complexity: Total memory storage required by the algorithm during execution (Instruction space + Data space + Dynamic space).
Fixed Space: Space for code, constants, and simple variables independent of input size n.
Variable Space: Dynamically allocated memory and call stack recursion space depending on n.
exam_tip: Highlight that space complexity includes auxiliary memory, not just input storage.

title: Best, Worst, and Average Case Complexity
badge: KTU Part A • 3 Marks • Bloom's K2
points: Worst-Case Complexity: Maximum number of steps taken on ANY input of size n (guaranteed upper bound performance).
Best-Case Complexity: Minimum number of steps taken on favorable input (e.g., finding key at index 0 in linear search = O(1)).
Average-Case Complexity: Expected number of steps over all possible inputs with probabilistic distribution.
University Standard: Unless specified otherwise, algorithmic analysis in KTU questions ALWAYS assumes Worst-Case.
code:
// Linear Search Cases:
Best Case: O(1) [Element at index 0]
Worst Case: O(n) [Element at index n-1 or absent]
Average Case: (n+1)/2 comparisons = O(n)
exam_tip: State the exact input condition that triggers best vs worst case.

title: Big-O Notation (O) — Upper Bound
badge: KTU Part A • 3 Marks • Bloom's K3
points: Formal Definition: f(n) = O(g(n)) if and only if there exist positive constants c and n0 such that f(n) <= c * g(n) for all n >= n0.
Interpretation: g(n) is an asymptotic upper bound for f(n). The function f(n) does not grow faster than g(n).
Worked Example: Prove 3n^2 + 5n + 7 = O(n^2).
Proof: For all n >= 1: 3n^2 + 5n + 7 <= 3n^2 + 5n^2 + 7n^2 = 15n^2. Thus c = 15 and n0 = 1 satisfy the definition.
exam_tip: Always specify the witness constants c and n0 in your proof to earn full marks.

title: Big-Omega Notation (Ω) — Lower Bound
badge: KTU Part A • 3 Marks • Bloom's K3
points: Formal Definition: f(n) = Ω(g(n)) if and only if there exist positive constants c and n0 such that f(n) >= c * g(n) for all n >= n0.
Interpretation: g(n) is an asymptotic lower bound for f(n). Algorithm takes at least this much time.
Worked Example: Prove 5n^2 - 3n = Ω(n^2).
Proof: For n >= 1: 5n^2 - 3n >= 5n^2 - 3n^2 = 2n^2. Choose c = 2 and n0 = 1. Therefore 5n^2 - 3n >= 2n^2.
exam_tip: Draw the growth curve showing f(n) staying above c * g(n) for n >= n0.

title: Big-Theta Notation (Θ) — Tight Bound
badge: KTU Part A • 3 Marks • Bloom's K3
points: Formal Definition: f(n) = Θ(g(n)) iff there exist positive constants c1, c2, and n0 such that c1*g(n) <= f(n) <= c2*g(n) for all n >= n0.
Interpretation: g(n) is an asymptotically tight bound. Both upper bound and lower bound match.
Theorem: f(n) = Θ(g(n)) if and only if f(n) = O(g(n)) AND f(n) = Ω(g(n)).
Worked Example: 7n + 5 = Θ(n) with c1 = 7, c2 = 12, n0 = 1.
exam_tip: State both upper bound c2 and lower bound c1 witness constants.

title: Little-o (o) and Little-omega (ω) Notations
badge: KTU Part A • 3 Marks • Bloom's K2
points: Little-o (o): f(n) = o(g(n)) if for ALL positive constants c > 0, there exists n0 such that f(n) < c * g(n) for all n >= n0.
Limit Definition: lim(n->inf) [f(n) / g(n)] = 0 (Strictly smaller growth rate).
Little-omega (ω): f(n) = ω(g(n)) if lim(n->inf) [f(n) / g(n)] = inf (Strictly greater growth rate).
Analogy: O is <=, o is <, Ω is >=, ω is >, and Θ is ==.
code:
// Limit Test for Asymptotic Notations:
lim(n->inf) f(n)/g(n) = 0   ==> f(n) = o(g(n))
lim(n->inf) f(n)/g(n) = c>0 ==> f(n) = Θ(g(n))
lim(n->inf) f(n)/g(n) = inf ==> f(n) = ω(g(n))
exam_tip: Use the limit definitions when asked to compare little-o vs Big-O in Part A.

title: Asymptotic Growth Hierarchy Ranking
points: Ascending Growth Rates: O(1) < O(log log n) < O(log n) < O(n^(1/c)) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n^2) < O(n^3) < O(2^n) < O(n!).
Polynomial vs Exponential: Any polynomial n^k is asymptotically strictly smaller than any exponential a^n (a > 1).
Logarithmic Property: log(n!) = Θ(n log n) via Stirling's Approximation.
Exam Pitfall: 2^(2n) = (2^n)^2 != O(2^n). But 2^(n+1) = 2 * 2^n = O(2^n).
code:
// Standard Asymptotic Ladder:
1 < log n < sqrt(n) < n < n log n < n^2 < n^3 < 2^n < n! < n^n
exam_tip: Memorize this ranking for Part A multiple-choice and short ordering questions.

points: Single Loop: for(i=0; i
Nested Independent: for(i=0; i
Triangular Loop: for(i=0; i
Multiplicative Loop: for(i=1; i
exam_tip: State both the loop step formula and the final asymptotic summation.

title: Step Count Method vs Operation Count Method
badge: KTU Part A • 3 Marks • Bloom's K2
points: Step Count: A count of the exact number of program execution steps executed regardless of hardware speed.
Operation Count: Counts specific active operations (e.g., number of comparisons, number of swaps, number of additions).
Step Table: Create a table with Statement, s/e (steps per execution), Frequency, and Total Steps.
University Utility: Used to derive exact linear equations like 3n + 2 prior to dropping constants for Big-O.
code:
// Step Table Structure:
Statement                  s/e    Frequency    Total Steps
for (i=0; i<n; i++)         1      n + 1        n + 1
    sum += a[i];            1      n            n
Total Program Steps: 2n + 1 = O(n)
exam_tip: Construct the 4-column step table in answers to secure full 3 marks.

title: Formulating Recurrence Relations for Recursive Code
points: Definition: An equation or inequality that describes a function in terms of its value on smaller inputs.
Base Case: T(n) = O(1) for n <= c (where subproblem size is solved directly without recursion).
Divide-and-Conquer Recurrence: T(n) = a T(n/b) + D(n) + C(n), where a = number of subproblems, n/b = subproblem size.
Work Breakdown: D(n) = division work, C(n) = combination work. Total non-recursive overhead f(n) = D(n) + C(n).
exam_tip: Always separate base condition from recursive definition in exam answers.

title: Substitution Method for Recurrences
points: Method: 1. Guess the form of the solution; 2. Use mathematical induction to find constants and prove correctness.
Problem: Solve T(n) = T(n-1) + n with T(1) = 1.
Back-Substitution: T(n) = T(n-2) + (n-1) + n = T(n-3) + (n-2) + (n-1) + n = ... = T(1) + 2 + 3 + ... + n.
Summation: T(n) = n(n+1)/2 = O(n^2).
exam_tip: Show at least 3 levels of expansion before generalizing to k.

title: Master Theorem — General Formulation
points: Applicability: For divide-and-conquer recurrences of form: T(n) = a T(n/b) + f(n), where a >= 1, b > 1, and f(n) > 0.
Critical Exponent: Compute watershed value log_b(a). The behavior depends on comparison between f(n) and n^(log_b(a)).
Case 1: f(n) = O(n^(log_b(a) - eps)) for eps > 0 ==> T(n) = Θ(n^(log_b(a))).
Case 2: f(n) = Θ(n^(log_b(a))) ==> T(n) = Θ(n^(log_b(a)) * log n).
Case 3: f(n) = Ω(n^(log_b(a) + eps)) and a*f(n/b) <= c*f(n) for c < 1 ==> T(n) = Θ(f(n)).
code:
// Master Theorem Parameters:
a: Number of subproblems (a >= 1)
b: Factor by which subproblem shrinks (b > 1)
f(n): Cost of divide and combine work
exam_tip: State the conditions on a and b (a >= 1, b > 1) to avoid 1-mark deduction.

title: Master Theorem — Case 1 Worked Problem
points: Recurrence: T(n) = 8 T(n/2) + 1000 n^2.
Parameters: a = 8, b = 2, f(n) = 1000 n^2.
Step 1: Compute log_b(a) = log_2(8) = 3 ==> n^(log_b(a)) = n^3.
Step 2: Compare f(n) = O(n^2) with n^3: n^2 = O(n^(3 - 1)) where eps = 1 > 0.
Conclusion: Subproblem work dominates. By Case 1: T(n) = Θ(n^3).
code:
// Verification:
log_2(8) = 3
f(n) = 1000 n^2 = O(n^(3 - eps)) for eps = 1
Result: T(n) = Θ(n^3)
exam_tip: Identify eps explicitly to prove it strictly falls into Case 1.

title: Master Theorem — Case 2 Worked Problem
points: Recurrence: T(n) = 2 T(n/2) + 5n (Merge Sort pattern).
Parameters: a = 2, b = 2, f(n) = 5n.
Step 1: Compute log_b(a) = log_2(2) = 1 ==> n^(log_b(a)) = n^1 = n.
Step 2: Compare f(n) = 5n = Θ(n^1). Both parts grow at the exact same rate.
Conclusion: Equal work across all recursion tree levels. By Case 2: T(n) = Θ(n log n).
code:
// Extended Case 2:
If f(n) = Θ(n^(log_b(a)) * log^k(n)) for k >= 0:
T(n) = Θ(n^(log_b(a)) * log^(k+1)(n))
For Merge Sort: k = 0 ==> T(n) = Θ(n log n)
exam_tip: This is the most frequent Master Theorem problem in KTU exams.

title: Master Theorem — Case 3 Worked Problem
points: Recurrence: T(n) = 2 T(n/2) + n^2.
Parameters: a = 2, b = 2, f(n) = n^2.
Step 1: log_b(a) = log_2(2) = 1 ==> n^(log_b(a)) = n.
Step 2: Compare f(n) = n^2 with n: n^2 = Ω(n^(1 + 1)) where eps = 1 > 0.
Step 3 (Regularity Check): a * f(n/b) <= c * f(n) ==> 2 * (n/2)^2 = 2 * n^2 / 4 = 0.5 n^2 <= 0.5 * f(n) for c = 0.5 < 1.
Conclusion: Root work dominates. By Case 3: T(n) = Θ(n^2).
code:
// Regularity Condition:
a * f(n/b) <= c * f(n) for c < 1
2 * (n/2)^2 = n^2 / 2 <= 0.5 * n^2 (Satisfied with c = 0.5)
Result: T(n) = Θ(n^2)
exam_tip: Do not forget the regularity check; KTU schemes reserve 2 marks specifically for this step.

title: Extended Master Theorem (Logarithmic Factors)
points: Limitation of Standard Theorem: Cannot solve T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n log n because n log n is asymptotically larger than n but not by a polynomial n^eps factor.
Extended Case 2 Formula: If f(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a) * log^k n):
- If k > -1: T(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a) * log^(k+1) n).
- If k = -1: T(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a) * log log n).
- If k < -1: T(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a)).
Solved Example: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n log n ==> a=2, b=2, k=1 ==> T(n) = Θ(n log^2 n).
code:
// Extended Case 2 Rule:
T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n log n
log_2(2) = 1 ==> f(n) = n^1 * log^1(n) [k=1]
==> T(n) = Θ(n * log^2(n))
exam_tip: Cite the Extended Master Theorem specifically when log factors appear in f(n).

title: Limitations of Master Theorem
badge: KTU Part A • 3 Marks • Bloom's K2
points: Condition 1: a is not a constant (e.g., T(n) = n T(n/2) + n).
Condition 2: a < 1 (non-sensical subproblem count).
Condition 3: f(n) is not polynomially bounded (e.g., T(n) = 2T(n/2) + 2^n).
Condition 4: Ratio f(n) / n^(log_b a) is not polynomial (e.g., T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n / log n).
Fallback: When Master Theorem fails, solve via Recursion Tree Method or Akra-Bazzi method.
code:
// Non-Applicable Recurrences:
T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n/log n  [f(n) is smaller by log, not n^eps]
T(n) = T(n-1) + n          [Subproblem is subtraction, not division]
T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n!        [f(n) factorial, not polynomial]
exam_tip: List at least 3 specific conditions where Master Theorem cannot be applied.

title: 2D Array Memory Representation — Row vs Column Major
badge: KTU Part A • 3 Marks • Bloom's K2
points: Linear Memory: Computer physical RAM is 1D linear array. 2D arrays A[M][N] must be linearized.
Row-Major Order (C/C++): Consecutive elements of the same row are stored contiguously in memory.
Row-Major Formula: Loc(A[i][j]) = Base + w * [ (i - lr) * N + (j - lc) ].
Column-Major Order (Fortran/MATLAB): Consecutive elements of same column stored contiguously.
Column-Major Formula: Loc(A[i][j]) = Base + w * [ (j - lc) * M + (i - lr) ].
code:
// Parameters:
Base: Starting memory address
w: Size of each element in bytes
lr, lc: Lower bounds of row and column (usually 0)
M, N: Total number of rows and columns
exam_tip: Always state the meaning of each variable (Base, w, M, N) in the formula.

title: 2D Array Address Calculation — Worked Numerical
points: Problem: Given array A[4..10][-2..5] stored in Row-Major order with Base Address 2000 and 4 bytes per element. Find address of A[7][2].
Step 1: Identify parameters: lr = 4, ur = 10 ==> M = 10 - 4 + 1 = 7 rows; lc = -2, uc = 5 ==> N = 5 - (-2) + 1 = 8 columns.
Step 2: Element size w = 4 bytes, Base = 2000.
code:
// Calculation Steps:
Rows M = 7, Columns N = 8
i - lr = 7 - 4 = 3
j - lc = 2 - (-2) = 4
Offset = (3 * 8 + 4) * 4 = 28 * 4 = 112
Address = 2000 + 112 = 2112
exam_tip: Double-check lower bound subtraction: j - (-2) becomes j + 2!

title: Polynomial Representation using Arrays
badge: KTU Part A • 3 Marks • Bloom's K2
points: Definition: Representing a mathematical polynomial P(x) = a_n x^n + ... + a_1 x + a_0 in memory.
Method 1 (Index as Exponent): Array index represents power, value represents coefficient. Wastes memory for sparse polynomials like x^1000 + 1.
Method 2 (Term Array): Array of structures storing only non-zero terms (coefficient, exponent).
C Structure: `typedef struct { float coeff; int expo; } Term; Term poly[MAX];`.
exam_tip: Highlight that descending exponent ordering is necessary for O(m+n) addition.

title: Algorithm: Polynomial Addition using Arrays
points: Principle: Merge two sorted term arrays A and B into result array C based on exponent comparison.
Case 1 (A[i].expo == B[j].expo): Add coefficients. If sum != 0, store in C[k] with matching expo. Increment i, j, k.
Case 2 (A[i].expo > B[j].expo): Copy term A[i] to C[k]. Increment i, k.
Case 3 (A[i].expo < B[j].expo): Copy term B[j] to C[k]. Increment j, k.
Remaining Terms: Copy any lingering terms from A or B once the other array terminates.
Time Complexity: O(m + n) where m and n are non-zero terms in A and B.
exam_tip: State that maximum terms in result polynomial is m + n.

title: Polynomial Addition — Step-by-Step Worked Example
points: Given Polynomials:
Step 1: Compare expo 3 vs 2: 3 > 2 ==> Copy (4,3) to C. i=1, j=0.
Step 2: Compare expo 2 vs 2: 2 == 2 ==> Add (3+2, 2) = (5,2) to C. i=2, j=1.
Step 3: Compare expo 0 vs 1: 0 < 1 ==> Copy (4,1) to C. i=2, j=2.
Step 4: Compare expo 0 vs 0: 0 == 0 ==> Add (5+1, 0) = (6,0) to C. i=3, j=3.
Result: C(x) = 4x^3 + 5x^2 + 4x + 6.
code:
// Result Term Array:
C = [ (4, 3), (5, 2), (4, 1), (6, 0) ]
Total Non-Zero Terms: 4
Total Comparisons: 4
exam_tip: Show the index pointers i, j, k at each step to earn full methodology marks.

title: Sparse Matrix Definition & Motivation
badge: KTU Part A • 3 Marks • Bloom's K2
points: Sparse Matrix: A matrix in which the majority of elements are ZERO.
Sparsity Ratio: Number of zero elements divided by total elements (typically > 75%).
Disadvantage of 2D Array: An m x n matrix requires m * n * sizeof(elem) memory, wasting 90%+ RAM on zero storage and wasting CPU cycles multiplying by zero.
Solution: Store only non-zero elements using 3-Tuple (Triplet) Representation or Linked Lists.
code:
// Memory Comparison for 1000 x 1000 matrix with 100 non-zero elements:
Standard 2D Array: 1000 * 1000 * 4 bytes = 4,000,000 bytes (4 MB)
3-Tuple Representation: (100 + 1) * 3 * 4 bytes = 1,212 bytes (1.2 KB)
Memory Savings: 99.97% reduction!
exam_tip: Quote real memory savings calculation in Part A to demonstrate deep understanding.

title: 3-Tuple (Coordinate / Triplet) Representation
points: Structure: A 2D array of (k + 1) rows and 3 columns [Row, Col, Value], where k is non-zero elements.
Row 0 (Header / Metadata):
- Row[0][0] = Total Rows in original matrix
- Row[0][1] = Total Columns in original matrix
- Row[0][2] = Total Non-Zero elements (k)
Rows 1 to k: Each row stores (row_index, col_index, non_zero_value) sorted in lexicographical order (row-major).
exam_tip: Remember: Row 0 is the metadata header; actual elements start at row 1!

title: Converting Matrix to 3-Tuple — Worked Example
points: Given 4 x 4 Matrix:
Non-Zero Count: 4 elements at (0,1)=10, (0,3)=12, (2,2)=5, (3,0)=15.
Resulting 3-Tuple Table:
Row 0: [ 4, 4, 4 ]  <-- Metadata (Rows, Cols, NonZeros)
code:
// 3-Tuple Matrix:
Index   Row   Col   Val
0        4     4     4
1        0     1    10
2        0     3    12
3        2     2     5
4        3     0    15
exam_tip: Make sure triplet rows are sorted primarily by row index, secondarily by col index.

title: Naive Transpose of Sparse Matrix
points: Principle: To transpose a matrix, swap rows and columns (Row <-> Col). The resulting triplets must remain sorted in row-major order.
Naive Algorithm: For each column c from 0 to total_cols - 1, scan all k triplets. If triplet has col == c, invert and write to result.
Outer Loop: Runs total_cols times.
Inner Loop: Scans all k non-zero elements.
Total Time Complexity: O(cols * k) = O(cols * non_zeros). In worst case (k ~ m*n), this degrades to O(cols^2 * rows).
exam_tip: State clearly why Naive Transpose is inefficient when column count is large.

title: Fast Transpose Algorithm — O(cols + non_zeros)
points: Key Idea: Eliminates nested loops by pre-calculating the EXACT destination index of each column in the transposed matrix.
Array 1: `row_terms[c]`: Counts the frequency of elements in column c.
Array 2: `starting_pos[c]`: Prefix sum of `row_terms`. `starting_pos[0] = 1`, `starting_pos[c] = starting_pos[c-1] + row_terms[c-1]`.
Single Pass Placement: For each element i in input array, find its destination index `pos = starting_pos[A[i].col]`, copy element, and increment `starting_pos[A[i].col]++`.
Time Complexity: O(cols + non_zeros) — strictly linear!
exam_tip: In 9-mark exams, you MUST show both the row_terms array and starting_pos array derivation.

title: Fast Transpose Worked Numerical: 4x4 Sparse Matrix
points: Given 4x4 sparse matrix with non-zeros: (0,1)=10, (0,3)=12, (2,2)=5, (3,0)=15.
Step 1: Compute `row_terms` for each col 0..3: `row_terms = [1, 1, 1, 1]`.
Step 2: Compute `starting_pos`: `starting_pos[0] = 1`, `starting_pos[1] = 1+1=2`, `starting_pos[2] = 2+1=3`, `starting_pos[3] = 3+1=4`.
Step 3: Single-pass placement into result array B.
code:
// Fast Transpose Computation:
row_terms:    [1, 1, 1, 1]
starting_pos: [1, 2, 3, 4]
After placing elements:
B[1] = (0, 3, 15)
B[2] = (1, 0, 10)
B[3] = (2, 2, 5)
B[4] = (3, 0, 12)
exam_tip: Construct both row_terms and starting_pos tables in your exam answer.

title: Fast Transpose vs Naive Transpose Comparison
points: Time Complexity: Naive is O(cols * elements); Fast Transpose is O(cols + elements).
Auxiliary Space: Naive uses O(1) extra space; Fast Transpose uses O(cols) for row_terms and starting_pos.
Loop Architecture: Naive uses nested loops (outer cols, inner elements); Fast Transpose uses 3 sequential linear loops.
Best Choice: Fast Transpose is vastly superior whenever matrix is large.
code:
// Comparison Matrix:
Feature          Naive Transpose         Fast Transpose
Time Complexity  O(cols * non_zeros)     O(cols + non_zeros)
Extra Space      O(1)                    O(cols)
Nested Loops?    Yes                     No (Linear passes)
exam_tip: Highlight that Fast Transpose trades O(cols) auxiliary memory for dramatic O(cols) speedup.

title: Sparse Matrix Addition: 3-Tuple Merge Algorithm
points: Principle: Merge two 3-tuple arrays A and B into result C based on lexicographical order of (row, col).
Case 1 (Same row and col): Add values. If sum != 0, store in C.
Case 2 (A has smaller row, or same row and smaller col): Copy A to C.
Case 3 (B has smaller row, or same row and smaller col): Copy B to C.
Time Complexity: O(non_zeros(A) + non_zeros(B)).
exam_tip: Do not insert element if the sum evaluates to zero!

title: Stack ADT: Definition, Axioms & LIFO Principle
badge: KTU Part A • 3 Marks • Bloom's K1
points: Definition: A linear data structure in which insertions and deletions take place at the same end called the TOP.
Discipline: Last-In, First-Out (LIFO). The most recently added element is the first one removed.
Core Operations: push(x) (insert item), pop() (delete and return top item), peek() (inspect top without deleting), isEmpty(), isFull().
Axiomatic Rule: pop(push(S, x)) = x.
exam_tip: Part A answers must include the LIFO expansion and all 5 primary operations.

title: Array Implementation of Stack: Push Operation
badge: KTU Part A / B • High-Yield Code
points: Precondition: Check if stack is full (Overflow condition).
Condition: `top == MAX - 1`.
Operation: Increment `top` pointer first, then assign value: `stack[++top] = x`.
Time Complexity: O(1) strictly constant time.
Space Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space.
exam_tip: Always perform the overflow check before writing to memory.

title: Array Implementation of Stack: Pop Operation
badge: KTU Part A / B • High-Yield Code
points: Precondition: Check if stack is empty (Underflow condition).
Condition: `top == -1`.
Operation: Retrieve value at `top`, then decrement pointer: `val = stack[top--]`.
Time Complexity: O(1) strictly constant time.
Space Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space.
exam_tip: Remember to return an error sentinel (like -1 or INT_MIN) on underflow.

title: Stack Overflow & Underflow Conditions & Boundary Cases
badge: KTU Part A • 3 Marks • Bloom's K2
points: Underflow: Occurs when `pop()` or `peek()` is invoked on an empty stack (`top == -1`). Attempting to read invalid memory.
Overflow: Occurs when `push(x)` is invoked on a completely filled fixed-size array stack (`top == MAX - 1`).
Dynamic Stack (Linked List): Underflow still exists, but Overflow only occurs if physical RAM is fully exhausted (malloc returns NULL).
code:
// Boundary Conditions:
isEmpty:  top == -1
isFull:   top == MAX - 1
Initial:  top = -1
exam_tip: State both array boundary indices: top == -1 and top == MAX - 1.

title: Two Stacks in a Single Array (Space Optimization)
points: Problem: Implement two stacks S1 and S2 in a single array of size N without wasting memory.
Design: S1 starts from left end (`top1 = -1`) and grows rightward (+1). S2 starts from right end (`top2 = N`) and grows leftward (-1).
Overflow Condition: When the two tops meet or collide: `top1 + 1 == top2`.
Underflow Conditions: S1 underflow: `top1 == -1`; S2 underflow: `top2 == N`.
Advantage: Stacks dynamically share array capacity; overflow occurs only when total elements equal N.
exam_tip: Draw the horizontal array with two opposing arrows pointing inward.

title: Multiple Stacks (k Stacks) in a Single Array
points: Method 1 (Fixed Partitioning): Divide array into k equal partitions of size N/k. Stack i bounded by [i*(N/k) .. (i+1)*(N/k)-1]. Disadvantage: Stack i can overflow even if adjacent partition is empty.
Method 2 (Dynamic with Linked Pointers): Maintain array `top[k]`, `next[N]`, and `free` pointer. Space-efficient and zero internal fragmentation.
Complexity: O(1) push and pop for all k stacks.
exam_tip: Mention the difference between fixed division and dynamic linked representation.

title: Application of Stacks: Balanced Parentheses Checking
points: Algorithm: Scan expression from left to right.
Opening bracket `(`, `{`, `[`: Push onto stack.
Closing bracket `)`, `}`, `]`: If stack is empty ==> Unbalanced! Else pop top element. If popped opening does not match closing ==> Unbalanced!
End of Expression: If stack is empty ==> Balanced! If stack is non-empty ==> Unbalanced (unclosed bracket)!
Time Complexity: O(n) linear scan. Space Complexity: O(n) stack memory.
exam_tip: The final check `return isEmpty()` is vital to catch unclosed opening brackets.

title: Balanced Parentheses Worked Trace: `{[()()]}` vs `{(])}`

1. `{` push; 2. `[` push; 3. `(` push; 4. `)` pop `(`, matches; 5. `(` push; 6. `)` pop `(`, matches; 7. `]` pop `[`, matches; 8. `}` pop `{`, matches. Stack empty ==> VALID!
Trace 2: `{(])}`
1. `{` push; 2. `(` push; 3. `]` pop `(`. Mismatch! `(` != `[` ==> INVALID (Mismatch error).

title: Infix, Prefix, and Postfix Notations
badge: KTU Part A • 3 Marks • Bloom's K2
points: Infix Notation: Operator placed between operands: `A + B`. Standard human notation, requires parentheses and precedence rules.
Prefix Notation (Polish): Operator placed before operands: `+ A B`. No parentheses needed; evaluated right-to-left.
Postfix Notation (Reverse Polish): Operator placed after operands: `A B +`. No parentheses needed; evaluated left-to-right using stack.
Why Compilers Convert to Postfix: Postfix eliminates ambiguity and parentheses, making computer stack evaluation instantaneous.

// Notation Equivalents:
Infix:   (A + B) * C
Prefix:  * + A B C
Postfix: A B + C *

title: Operator Precedence & Associativity Table
points: Compilers and conversion algorithms require precise precedence values.
Exponentiation `^`: Precedence 3, Right-to-Left associativity (e.g. 2^3^2 = 2^(3^2) = 512).
Multiplication `*` and Division `/`: Precedence 2, Left-to-Right associativity.
Addition `+` and Subtraction `-`: Precedence 1, Left-to-Right associativity.
Parentheses `(`: Highest priority outside stack, lowest priority inside stack.
exam_tip: Crucial exam rule: `^` has RIGHT-TO-LEFT associativity; all others are Left-to-Right.

title: Infix to Postfix Algorithm (Shunting-Yard Stack Algorithm)
points: Algorithm: Scan infix from left to right.
1. Operand: Immediately output to postfix string.
2. Left Parenthesis `(`: Push onto stack.
3. Right Parenthesis `)`: Pop and output from stack until `(` is popped. Discard `(`.
4. Operator: While stack not empty and prec(stack[top]) >= prec(c) (or > if `^`), pop and output. Then push current operator.
5. End of String: Pop and output all remaining operators on stack.
exam_tip: Never output parentheses `(` or `)` into the final postfix string!

11. `)` -> pop `-` -> out `A B C D ^ E -`, pop `(`
Final Result: `A B C D ^ E - * F G H * + / +`.

When scanning second `^`, do NOT pop first `^` because right-associative operators are pushed when equal precedence occurs.

title: Evaluation of Postfix Expression: Algorithm & Stack Mechanism
points: Algorithm: Scan postfix expression from left to right.
1. Operand: Push value onto stack.
2. Operator: Pop two operands from stack:
`val2 = pop();` (Top element is SECOND operand!)
`val1 = pop();` (Next element is FIRST operand!)
3. Compute: `result = val1 (operator) val2`.
4. Push result back onto stack.
5. At end of expression: The single remaining element on stack is the FINAL VALUE!
exam_tip: CRITICAL RULE: First pop is operand 2; second pop is operand 1! Swapping causes error on `-` and `/`.

title: Queue ADT: Definition, Axioms & FIFO Principle
badge: KTU Part A • 3 Marks • Bloom's K1
points: Definition: A linear data structure in which insertions take place at one end called the REAR, and deletions take place at the opposite end called the FRONT.
Discipline: First-In, First-Out (FIFO). The first element inserted is the first element to be removed.
Core Operations: enqueue(x) (insert at rear), dequeue() (delete from front), frontElement(), isEmpty(), isFull().
Real-world Examples: CPU task scheduling, print spooler queue, customer service line.
exam_tip: Contrast FIFO with Stack's LIFO in Part A.

title: Array Implementation of Linear Queue
badge: KTU Part A / B • High-Yield Code
points: Variables: `front` points to first element; `rear` points to last element. Initial: `front = -1, rear = -1`.
Enqueue(x): Check overflow (`rear == MAX - 1`). If empty, `front = 0`. Increment `rear`, `arr[++rear] = x`.
Dequeue(): Check underflow (`front == -1 || front > rear`). Retrieve `arr[front++]`. If `front > rear`, reset both to -1.
Time Complexity: O(1) for both enqueue and dequeue.
exam_tip: Remember the reset step: if front > rear, set front = rear = -1.

title: Drawbacks of Linear Queue: False Overflow (Memory Wastage)
badge: KTU Part A • 3 Marks • Bloom's K2
points: The Problem: In a linear queue, when elements are repeatedly enqueued and dequeued, `rear` eventually reaches `MAX - 1`.
False Overflow: Even if slots at the beginning of the array are completely free (vacated by earlier dequeues), `enqueue()` reports OVERFLOW because `rear == MAX - 1`!
Memory Wastage: Unusable free memory slots accumulate on the left.
Solution: Circular Queue where the array wraps around in a circle.
exam_tip: Illustrate with an array diagram showing empty front slots.

title: Circular Queue Concept & Clockwise Index Arithmetic
points: Principle: Treats the linear array as a circular ring where index 0 immediately follows index `MAX - 1`.
Clockwise Step: Incrementation uses modulo arithmetic: `next_index = (index + 1) % MAX`.
Eliminates False Overflow: Freely reuses slots at index 0 after elements are dequeued.
Capacity: A circular queue of array size MAX can store at most `MAX - 1` elements (reserving 1 empty slot to distinguish full from empty).
exam_tip: State the modulo formula: `(index + 1) % MAX`.

title: Circular Queue Overflow & Underflow Conditions
points: Underflow Condition: Occurs when queue contains zero elements. Standard condition: `front == -1`.
Overflow Condition: Occurs when advancing `rear` by 1 clockwise hits `front`.
Formula: `(rear + 1) % MAX == front`.
Alternative Formula: `(front == 0 && rear == MAX - 1) || (front == rear + 1)`.
Capacity: Storing n elements requires an array of size n+1 to avoid ambiguity.
code:
// Circular Queue Conditions:
Underflow: front == -1
Overflow:  (rear + 1) % MAX == front
Initial:   front = -1, rear = -1
exam_tip: Write the single unified overflow condition: `(rear + 1) % MAX == front`.

title: Circular Queue: Enqueue Algorithm & Code
points: Algorithm: 1. Check if full: `if ((rear + 1) % MAX == front) return Overflow;`
2. If empty (`front == -1`), set `front = rear = 0;`
3. Else increment rear circularly: `rear = (rear + 1) % MAX;`
4. Store element: `queue[rear] = x;`
Time Complexity: O(1) strictly constant time.
exam_tip: Always test for empty queue condition `front == -1` to initialize front to 0.

title: Circular Queue: Dequeue Algorithm & Code
points: Algorithm: 1. Check if empty: `if (front == -1) return Underflow;`
2. Retrieve data: `val = queue[front];`
3. If single element remaining (`front == rear`), reset queue: `front = rear = -1;`
4. Else increment front circularly: `front = (front + 1) % MAX;`
5. Return val. Time Complexity: O(1).
exam_tip: Do not forget the reset check `front == rear` when the last element is deleted.

title: Double-Ended Queue (Deque): Types & Operations
badge: KTU Part A • 3 Marks • Bloom's K2
points: Definition: A linear list in which elements can be added or removed at EITHER end (Front or Rear).
Input-Restricted Deque: Insertion allowed at only ONE end (Rear); Deletion allowed at BOTH ends (Front & Rear).
Output-Restricted Deque: Deletion allowed at only ONE end (Front); Insertion allowed at BOTH ends (Front & Rear).
Four Primary Operations: insertFront(), insertRear(), deleteFront(), deleteRear().

Order of Departure: Not purely FIFO; determined by priority key (ties resolved via FIFO).
Array Representation 1 (Unordered Array): Enqueue O(1); Dequeue scans for maximum priority O(n).
Array Representation 2 (Ordered Array): Enqueue inserts in sorted order O(n); Dequeue removes from end O(1).

title: Reversing a Queue using a Stack
points: Principle: Queue is FIFO; Stack is LIFO. Passing elements through a stack inverts their order!
Algorithm:
Step 1: While queue is not empty, dequeue each element and push onto stack.
Step 2: While stack is not empty, pop each element from stack and enqueue back into queue.
Result: Queue elements are now in exactly reversed order!
Complexity: Time O(n) linear; Space O(n) stack memory.
exam_tip: Draw the 2-stage transfer diagram (Queue -> Stack -> Queue).

title: Implementing Stack using Two Queues
points: Method 1 (Costly Push):
- Push(x): 1. Enqueue x to Q2; 2. Dequeue all elements of Q1 and enqueue to Q2; 3. Swap names of Q1 and Q2.
- Pop(): Dequeue from Q1. Time: O(1).
Method 2 (Costly Pop):
- Push(x): Enqueue x to Q1. Time: O(1).
- Pop(): Move n-1 elements from Q1 to Q2. Dequeue the remaining element from Q1 (which is the top element!). Swap names. Time: O(n).
exam_tip: Contrast Costly Push (O(n) push, O(1) pop) with Costly Pop (O(1) push, O(n) pop).

title: Implementing Queue using Two Stacks
points: Design: Uses two stacks S1 (inbox) and S2 (outbox).
Enqueue(x): Simply push x onto S1: `push(S1, x)`. Time: O(1).
Dequeue():
- If both S1 and S2 are empty: Underflow!
- If S2 is empty: Transfer ALL elements from S1 to S2 by popping from S1 and pushing to S2 (inverting LIFO into FIFO!).
- Pop and return from S2: `return pop(S2);`.
Amortized Complexity: Each element is pushed twice and popped twice, yielding Amortized O(1) time per operation!

title: Dynamic Memory Allocation vs Static Memory Allocation
badge: KTU Part A • 3 Marks • Bloom's K2
points: Static Allocation: Memory allocated at compile time on Stack/Data segment; fixed size (e.g., int arr[100]).
Dynamic Allocation: Memory allocated at runtime on Heap using malloc(), calloc(), realloc(), free().
Flexibility: Dynamic allocation allows data structures to grow and shrink dynamically based on actual demand.
Memory Deallocation: Static is automatically freed when scope ends; Dynamic requires explicit free() to avoid memory leaks.
exam_tip: Mention Stack vs Heap memory location in your answer.

title: Singly Linked List (SLL) Node Structure & Memory Model
badge: KTU Part A • 3 Marks • Bloom's K1
points: Definition: A linear collection of data elements called nodes, where linear order is given by pointers.
Node Structure: Contains at least two fields: 1. `data` (payload); 2. `next` (pointer storing memory address of next node).
Head Pointer: Stores memory address of the first node. If list is empty, `head == NULL`.
Tail Node: The final node whose `next` pointer contains `NULL` (sentinel terminator).
exam_tip: Define self-referential structure in Part A answers.

title: Array vs Linked List Comprehensive Comparison
points: Memory Allocation: Array is contiguous static/dynamic; Linked List is non-contiguous dynamic.
Insertion/Deletion at Beginning: Array is O(n) (requires shifting); Linked List is O(1) (pointer redirect).
Random Access: Array is O(1) (direct index arithmetic); Linked List is O(n) (sequential traversal).
Memory Overhead: Array has zero per-element pointer overhead; Linked List requires 4-8 bytes pointer per node.
Cache Locality: Array has excellent spatial locality; Linked List has poor cache performance.
code:
// Comparison Summary:
Feature          Array          Linked List
Access Time      O(1)           O(n)
Insert at Head   O(n)           O(1)
Insert at Tail   O(1)*          O(n) / O(1) with tail
Memory Overhead  Zero           Pointer per node
Resize Cost      O(n) realloc   O(1) dynamic
exam_tip: Draw this 5-row comparison table for 3-mark or 9-mark comparison questions.

title: SLL Insertion at Beginning: Algorithm & Analysis
badge: KTU Part A / B • High-Yield Code
points: Algorithm: 1. Allocate new node; 2. Assign `newNode->data = val`; 3. `newNode->next = head`; 4. `head = newNode`.
Order of Pointer Updates: Must set `newNode->next = head` BEFORE updating `head = newNode`, otherwise existing list is lost!
Time Complexity: O(1) constant time — zero shifting required.
Space Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space.
exam_tip: Highlight that no traversal is needed, giving guaranteed O(1) efficiency.

title: SLL Insertion at End: Algorithm & Analysis
points: Algorithm: 1. Allocate new node with `next = NULL`; 2. If list empty (`head == NULL`), set `head = newNode` and return.
Traversal: If list non-empty, traverse with pointer `curr` until `curr->next == NULL`.
Linking: Set `curr->next = newNode`.
Time Complexity: O(n) traversal time (or O(1) if separate `tail` pointer maintained).
exam_tip: Show the empty list check `if (head == NULL)` to avoid NULL pointer dereference crash.

title: SLL Insertion After a Given Node
points: Given: Pointer `prevNode` to an existing node in the list.
Validation: Check `if (prevNode == NULL)` ==> Cannot insert.
Pointer Updates:
1. `newNode->next = prevNode->next;` (Connect new node to downstream list)
2. `prevNode->next = newNode;` (Connect upstream node to new node)
Time Complexity: O(1) once `prevNode` is located.
exam_tip: Draw the two arrow redirects: first new->next, then prev->next.

title: SLL Deletion at Beginning
badge: KTU Part A • 3 Marks • Bloom's K2
points: Algorithm: 1. Check if empty (`head == NULL`); 2. Store `temp = head`; 3. `head = head->next`; 4. `free(temp)`.
Memory Deallocation: Must call `free(temp)` in C to prevent memory leak.
Edge Cases: Empty list (underflow error), single-element list (head becomes NULL).
Time Complexity: O(1) constant time.
exam_tip: Always store head in a temporary pointer before advancing head!

title: SLL Deletion at End
points: Algorithm:
- Case 1 (Empty): `head == NULL` ==> Return underflow.
- Case 2 (Single Node): `head->next == NULL` ==> `free(head); head = NULL; return;`.
- Case 3 (Multiple Nodes): Traverse with `curr` until `curr->next->next == NULL` (second to last node).
Pointer Update: `free(curr->next); curr->next = NULL;`.
Time Complexity: O(n) traversal time.
exam_tip: Notice the loop condition `curr->next->next != NULL` to stop at second-to-last node.

title: SLL Deletion of a Specific Node by Key
points: Algorithm: Search for node containing `key` while tracking predecessor pointer `prev`.
Case 1 (Head Node matches): `head = head->next; free(temp); return;`.
Case 2 (Internal/Tail Node matches): `prev->next = curr->next; free(curr);`.
Case 3 (Key Not Found): `curr == NULL` ==> Print 'Key absent'.
Time Complexity: O(n) search time.
exam_tip: Show both prev and curr pointers in your trace diagram.

title: Searching an Element in Singly Linked List
points: Sequential traversal comparing each node's data. Best O(1), Worst O(n). Binary search impossible due to lack of random access.
exam_tip: Explain why Binary Search CANNOT be applied to Singly Linked List.

title: Counting Nodes & Finding Middle of SLL
points: Slow & Fast Pointer (Tortoise & Hare): slow moves 1 step, fast moves 2 steps. When fast reaches end, slow is at middle! O(n) single pass.
exam_tip: State that the two-pointer approach finds middle in a single pass without prior length count.

title: Reversing a Singly Linked List (Iterative Algorithm)
points: 3-Pointer Technique: prev = NULL, curr = head, next = NULL. In loop: next = curr->next; curr->next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next. Finally head = prev.
exam_tip: In 9-mark exams, draw the pointer redirect diagram for at least 3 nodes.

title: Reversing a SLL — Step-by-Step Diagram Trace
points: Trace reversing 10 -> 20 -> 30 -> NULL. Show prev, curr, next at each of the 3 iterations. Final head points to 30.
code:
// Trace Table:
Init:  prev=NULL, curr=10
Iter1: 10->next=NULL; prev=10, curr=20
Iter2: 20->next=10;   prev=20, curr=30
Iter3: 30->next=20;   prev=30, curr=NULL
End:   head = prev = 30
exam_tip: Label each pointer clearly to get all 4 diagram marks.

title: Reversing a Singly Linked List (Recursive Algorithm)
points: Divide into first node and rest of list. Recursively reverse rest. Link rest->next = head; head->next = NULL. Time O(n), Space O(n) call stack.
exam_tip: Highlight the crucial step: `node->next->next = node` to reverse direction.

title: Detecting Cycle/Loop in SLL (Floyd's Algorithm)
points: Tortoise & Hare: slow moves 1 step, fast moves 2 steps. If cycle exists, fast will lap slow and slow == fast. If no cycle, fast reaches NULL. O(n) time, O(1) space.
exam_tip: Mention that Floyd's algorithm requires strictly O(1) auxiliary space.

title: Finding the Starting Node of Loop in SLL
points: After collision point, reset slow to head. Keep fast at collision. Advance both 1 step at a time. The point where they meet is the start of loop! Proof: 2(F + a) = F + a + nC ==> F = nC - a.
exam_tip: Include the algebraic proof (F = C - a) for full marks.

title: Merging Two Sorted Singly Linked Lists
points: Compare head elements of lists A and B. Attach smaller to result list. Advance that list. When one list empty, attach remainder of other. Time O(m + n), Space O(1).
exam_tip: Show that merging does not create new nodes; it rewires existing pointers.

title: Polynomial Representation using Singly Linked List
points: Each node stores: float coeff, int expo, struct Node *next. Nodes ordered in descending order of exponents. Allows arbitrary degree polynomials without memory waste.
exam_tip: Highlight that exponents need not be contiguous, solving array sparsity.

title: Algorithm: Polynomial Addition using Linked List
points: Traverse lists p1 and p2. Compare exponents: equal ==> add coeffs; p1->expo > p2->expo ==> insert p1 term; else ==> insert p2 term. O(m + n) time.
exam_tip: State what happens when sum of coefficients equals zero (do not insert).

title: Stack Implementation using Singly Linked List
points: Push: insertAtBeginning(x) O(1). Pop: deleteFromBeginning() O(1). Peek: return head->data O(1). Never overflows unless heap exhausted.
code:
void push(int x) { struct Node* n = malloc(sizeof(*n)); n->data = x; n->next = top; top = n; }
int pop() { if(!top) return -1; struct Node* t = top; int v = t->data; top = top->next; free(t); return v; }
exam_tip: Explain why Top is maintained at head, not at tail (O(1) vs O(n) pop).

title: Queue Implementation using Singly Linked List
points: Maintain two pointers: front and rear. Enqueue: insertAtEnd(rear) O(1). Dequeue: deleteFromBeginning(front) O(1). No false overflow.
exam_tip: Show the empty queue case where both front and rear are updated.

title: Doubly Linked List (DLL) Node Structure & Properties
points: Node has 3 fields: prev pointer, data payload, next pointer. Bidirectional traversal (forward & backward). Memory overhead: 2 pointers per node.
exam_tip: State that head->prev == NULL and tail->next == NULL.

title: Advantages and Disadvantages of Doubly Linked List
points: Advantages: Bidirectional traversal, O(1) node deletion given node pointer without traversing to predecessor. Disadvantages: Extra memory (prev pointer), extra pointer updates on insert/delete.
exam_tip: Give both 2 advantages and 2 disadvantages for 3 marks.

title: DLL Insertion at Beginning
points: 1. newNode->next = head; 2. newNode->prev = NULL; 3. if (head != NULL) head->prev = newNode; 4. head = newNode. Time: O(1).
exam_tip: Remember to check `if (head != NULL)` before updating `head->prev`!

title: DLL Insertion at End
points: Traverse to last node `curr`. 1. newNode->next = NULL; 2. newNode->prev = curr; 3. curr->next = newNode. If list empty, head = newNode. Time: O(n).
exam_tip: Show both the next and prev link updates between curr and newNode.

title: DLL Insertion Before a Given Node (4-Way Pointer Rewiring)
points: Given node `curr`. 1. newNode->next = curr; 2. newNode->prev = curr->prev; 3. if (curr->prev) curr->prev->next = newNode else head = newNode; 4. curr->prev = newNode.
exam_tip: This is a 9-mark KTU favorite. Draw the 4 numbered arrows in your diagram.

title: DLL Deletion of a Given Node
points: Given pointer to node `del`. 1. If del == head: head = del->next; 2. if (del->next) del->next->prev = del->prev; 3. if (del->prev) del->prev->next = del->next; 4. free(del). O(1) time!
exam_tip: Contrast with SLL: DLL deletes in O(1) because del->prev is directly accessible!

title: Circular Singly Linked List (CSLL) & Last Pointer
points: Last node points back to first node (no NULL). Best practice: maintain `last` pointer instead of `head`. last->next is head! Gives O(1) insertion at both head and tail.
exam_tip: Explain why maintaining `last` is superior to maintaining `head` in CSLL.

title: Circular Singly Linked List Operations
points: Insert at Beginning: newNode->next = last->next; last->next = newNode. Insert at End: newNode->next = last->next; last->next = newNode; last = newNode! Both O(1)!
exam_tip: Point out that insertEnd and insertBeginning share 90% of the exact same code.

title: Circular Doubly Linked List (CDLL)
points: head->prev points to last node; last->next points to head. Bidirectional endless ring. Used in OS process round robin scheduling and media playlists.
exam_tip: State the two boundary invariants for CDLL.

title: Header Linked Lists (Grounded vs Circular)
points: Header list contains a dummy header node at beginning storing metadata (e.g., node count). Grounded: last node points to NULL. Circular: last node points to header.
exam_tip: Mention that dummy header node eliminates special case code for inserting at head.

title: Josephus Problem Solved via Circular Linked List
points: N people in circle, eliminate every M-th person until 1 survives. Solved by creating CSLL of N nodes, skipping M-1 nodes, deleting M-th node repeatedly. O(N * M) time.
exam_tip: State the base mathematical recurrence: J(n, 2) = 2(n - 2^floor(log2 n)) + 1.

title: Dynamic Memory Allocation in Operating Systems
points: OS divides RAM into System space and User heap space. When processes request memory via malloc()/new, memory manager searches free memory list for suitable hole.
code:
// Memory Request Flow:
User: malloc(size) -> Heap Allocator (brk/sbrk) -> Search Free List -> Split Block -> Return Pointer
exam_tip: Explain what a 'hole' is (a contiguous block of free unallocated memory).

title: Free List Representation & Data Structures
points: Linked list of free memory holes. Each hole node stores: Base Address, Size of Block, Next Pointer. Holes are maintained ordered by address, size, or allocation recency.
exam_tip: State that free list nodes reside inside the free memory blocks themselves.

title: First-Fit Memory Allocation Scheme
points: Search free list from beginning. Allocate the FIRST hole that is large enough (size >= request). Split hole if larger. Fast search O(n), but tends to cluster small fragments at beginning of heap.
exam_tip: First-Fit is generally the fastest allocation heuristic in practice.

title: Best-Fit Memory Allocation Scheme
points: Search ENTIRE free list. Allocate the SMALLEST hole that is large enough (min(hole_size - request) >= 0). Goal: minimize wasted space. Drawback: creates tiny, unusable sliver fragments.
exam_tip: Best-Fit requires scanning the entire list unless organized as a balanced tree.

title: Worst-Fit Memory Allocation Scheme
points: Search ENTIRE free list. Allocate the LARGEST available hole. Goal: leftover fragment is large enough to remain useful for subsequent requests. Drawback: destroys large holes quickly.
exam_tip: Worst-Fit aims to produce large remainders, but rapidly depletes big memory blocks.

title: Next-Fit Memory Allocation Scheme
points: Variant of First-Fit. Rather than restarting search from head of free list each time, search begins where previous search ended (roving pointer). Spreads fragments across entire heap.
code:
// Next-Fit Pointer:
static struct FreeHole *last_alloc_ptr = NULL;
exam_tip: Next-Fit avoids the front-of-list fragmentation concentration of First-Fit.

title: Memory Allocation Numerical: First-Fit vs Best-Fit vs Worst-Fit
points: Holes: 100K, 500K, 200K, 300K, 600K. Requests: 212K, 417K, 112K, 426K. First-Fit puts 212K in 500K, 417K in 600K, 112K in 288K hole, 426K waits. Best-Fit puts 212K in 300K, 417K in 500K, 112K in 200K, 426K in 600K (All succeed!).
code:
// Best-Fit Outcome:
212K -> 300K (leaves 88K)
417K -> 500K (leaves 83K)
112K -> 200K (leaves 88K)
426K -> 600K (leaves 174K)
All 4 processes allocated successfully!
exam_tip: Construct the detailed 5-column trace table in your answer sheet.

title: Internal Fragmentation: Definition, Cause & Formula
points: Memory allocated to process is larger than requested memory. Occurs due to fixed partitioning or alignment padding (e.g. 4-byte/8-byte word boundaries). Internal Frag = Allocated - Requested.
exam_tip: Contrast: Internal is inside allocated block; External is outside between blocks.

title: External Fragmentation: Definition & Formula
points: Total free memory space is sufficient to satisfy request, but memory is non-contiguous (fragmented into small holes), so request cannot be fulfilled. Ext Frag = 1 - (Max_Block / Total_Free).
exam_tip: Quote the external fragmentation ratio formula to earn full 3 marks.

title: The 50% Rule in Memory Management
points: Knuth's 50% Rule: In any dynamic memory allocation system using First-Fit, for every N allocated blocks, there will be approximately 0.5 N free holes due to fragmentation.
exam_tip: Cite Donald Knuth's 50% rule when discussing First-Fit performance.

title: Buddy System Memory Allocation
points: Memory is partitioned into blocks of size 2^k. When request of size s arrives, find smallest power of 2 >= s. If current block too large, recursively split into two equal 'buddies' of size 2^(k-1).
code:
// Buddy Splitting:
1024K block split into two 512K buddies.
512K split into two 256K buddies.
Coalescing: When both buddies free, merge back to 512K!
exam_tip: Explain that buddy address differs by exactly 1 bit: Buddy_Addr = Addr XOR (1 << k).

title: Buddy System Worked Trace Example
points: Total memory 1024 KB. Trace requests: A=100K, B=240K, C=64K, Release A, Release B. Show binary tree splits and buddy coalescing merges.
code:
// Allocation Tree:
1024K -> [512K, 512K]
512K -> [256K, 256K]
256K -> [128K, 128K] ==> Allocate A in 128K
B allocated in 256K; C allocated in 64K
exam_tip: Draw the binary tree buddy diagram showing splits and merges.

title: Memory Compaction (Defragmentation)
points: Moving all allocated memory blocks to one end of memory and combining all free holes into one large contiguous block. Requires dynamic relocatable address binding (base register).
exam_tip: State the prerequisite: Compaction is ONLY possible if program uses dynamic runtime address binding!

title: Compaction Approaches: Two-Finger vs LISP 2 Algorithm
points: Two-Finger Algorithm: Moves blocks from end of memory into holes at front (high relocation cost, changes order). Sliding Compaction (LISP 2): Preserves block order by sliding all blocks to low addresses.
code:
// Sliding Compaction Phases:
1. Compute new addresses
2. Update all pointers
3. Slide data blocks
exam_tip: Mention that sliding compaction preserves pointer order and relative locality.

title: SLAB Allocation in Linux Kernel
points: Specialized caching allocator for kernel objects (semaphores, file descriptors, task_struct). Eliminates fragmentation by pre-allocating contiguous pages into slabs of identical object sizes.
exam_tip: SLAB allocator avoids fragmentation by grouping identical-sized objects together.

title: Memory Leaks and Dangling Pointers
points: Memory Leak: Dynamically allocated memory that is no longer referenced but never freed with free(). Dangling Pointer: A pointer that still points to a memory address that has already been deallocated.
exam_tip: Always set pointer to NULL after freeing: `free(p); p = NULL;`.

title: Boundary Tag Method for Memory Coalescing
points: Knuth's Boundary Tag: Every block stores header and footer containing size and allocation flag (alloc/free). Allows O(1) coalescing with both left and right adjacent neighbors upon free().
exam_tip: Boundary tags enable constant-time O(1) bidirectional neighbor coalescing.

title: What is Garbage in Computer Memory?
points: Garbage refers to dynamically allocated heap memory objects that are unreachable by any active program reference (root set) but occupy physical RAM.
exam_tip: Define 'Root Set' (global variables, local stack frame variables, CPU registers).

title: Garbage Collection (GC) Principles & Root Set
points: Automatic reclamation of unused heap memory. Root Set: Starting pointers directly accessible to program without traversing heap (registers, stack variables, global variables).
code:
// Liveness Definition:
An object is LIVE if it is in Root Set OR reachable via chain of pointers from Root Set.
exam_tip: Objects not reachable from roots are guaranteed dead and can be collected.

title: Reference Counting Garbage Collection Algorithm
points: Each object maintains an integer `ref_count`. When new pointer references object: `ref_count++`. When pointer removed: `ref_count--`. If `ref_count == 0` ==> Reclaim immediately.
exam_tip: Immediate reclamation on ref_count == 0 is the primary advantage.

title: The Fatal Flaw of Reference Counting: Circular References
points: Two objects reference each other: A->next = B and B->next = A. When external pointer is removed, ref_count of both remains 1! They are unreachable from roots but NEVER freed.
code:
// Island of Isolation:
A.ref_count = 1 (held by B)
B.ref_count = 1 (held by A)
External pointers: NULL ==> Permanent memory leak!
exam_tip: Draw the circular reference diagram showing island of isolation.

title: Mark-and-Sweep Garbage Collection Algorithm
points: Two-Phase Tracing Collector: Phase 1 (Mark): Start from roots, traverse graph via DFS/BFS, set mark_bit = 1 for all reachable objects. Phase 2 (Sweep): Scan entire heap linearly. If mark_bit == 0 ==> Free to free-list. Else reset mark_bit = 0.
exam_tip: State both phases clearly: Phase 1 (Marking reachable) and Phase 2 (Sweeping unmarked).

title: Mark-and-Sweep Advantages & Disadvantages
points: Advantages: Handles circular references perfectly; no runtime overhead on pointer assignment. Disadvantages: Stop-the-world pause; fragmentation remains; sweep phase scans entire heap O(heap_size).
code:
// Comparison vs Ref Counting:
Feature           Ref Counting   Mark-and-Sweep
Circular Refs     FAILS          HANDLES
Pause Times       Incremental    Stop-the-world
Heap Fragmentation Leaves holes   Leaves holes
exam_tip: Mention 'Stop-The-World' execution pause in disadvantages.

title: Stop-and-Copy (Copying) Garbage Collector
points: Heap divided into From-Space and To-Space. When From-Space fills, traverse live objects from roots and copy them compactly into To-Space. Swap space roles. Free From-Space en masse. Zero fragmentation!
code:
// Copying GC Flow:
From-Space: [Live1][Dead][Live2][Dead] (Fragmented)
To-Space:   [Live1][Live2][--- FREE ALL CONTIGUOUS ---]
Swap From-Space <-> To-Space
exam_tip: Copying GC automatically compacts memory during collection!

title: Generational Garbage Collection
points: Weak Generational Hypothesis: Most objects die young (temporary variables, loop iterators). Divide heap into Young Generation (Eden + Survivor spaces) and Old/Tenured Generation. Minor GC collects young frequently and fast.
code:
// Generational Architecture:
[Eden (New Objects)] -> [Survivor S0, S1] -> [Tenured (Promoted Long-Lived)]
Minor GC: Fast copy of Eden to Survivor
Major GC: Infrequent full Mark-and-Sweep of Tenured
exam_tip: Quote the Weak Generational Hypothesis in your explanation.

title: Baker's Incremental Garbage Collection
points: Real-time garbage collector that interleaves collection steps with user program execution to bound maximum pause time. Uses tricolor marking (White = unvisited, Grey = visited children unvisited, Black = visited children visited).
code:
// Tricolor Invariant:
No Black object points directly to a White object without an intervening Grey object.
exam_tip: Tricolor abstraction is the foundation of concurrent and incremental GC.

title: Comparison Table: Garbage Collection Algorithms
points: Ref Counting (Instant, fails cycles, assignments slow); Mark-Sweep (Handles cycles, pauses, fragments); Copying (Compacts, fast allocate, halves memory); Generational (Best performance, tuned for lifetimes).
code:
// Master GC Comparison:
Algorithm      Cycle Handling   Compaction   Pause Time
Ref Count      No               No           Zero
Mark-Sweep     Yes              No           High
Stop-Copy      Yes              Yes          Medium
Generational   Yes              Yes (Young)  Low
exam_tip: Draw this 4-row matrix for any comparative GC question.

title: Finding N-th Node from End of Singly Linked List
points: Two-pointer technique: Advance first pointer n steps ahead. Then move both first and second pointers 1 step together until first reaches NULL. Second pointer points to n-th from end! O(n) single pass.
exam_tip: Single-pass algorithm is expected; do not count length first and traverse twice!

title: Palindrome Checking in a Singly Linked List
points: 1. Find middle using slow/fast pointers; 2. Reverse second half of list; 3. Compare first half and second half data node-by-node; 4. (Optional) Restore second half. O(n) time, O(1) space.
code:
// Palindrome Steps:
1. Middle = findMiddle(head)
2. RevSecond = reverse(Middle)
3. Check head->data == RevSecond->data
Result: boolean isPalin
exam_tip: Show how O(1) auxiliary space is maintained by reversing in-place.

title: Flattening a Multilevel Linked List
points: Each node has data, next pointer, and child pointer to a sub-linked list. Flatten into single linear list. Use tail pointer: append child lists to tail of main list. O(n) time.
exam_tip: Trace how child pointers are converted into next pointers.

title: Memory Footprint Derivation: SLL vs DLL vs Array
points: For 10,000 integer elements on 64-bit architecture: Array = 10000 * 4 = 40 KB. SLL = 10000 * (4 data + 4 padding + 8 next) = 160 KB (4x). DLL = 10000 * (4 data + 4 pad + 8 next + 8 prev) = 240 KB (6x).
code:
// Memory Footprint (64-bit aligned):
Array:  40,000 bytes (1x)
SLL:   160,000 bytes (4x overhead)
DLL:   240,000 bytes (6x overhead)
exam_tip: Include compiler struct alignment padding (4 bytes) in 64-bit derivations.

title: Skip Lists: Concept & Search Efficiency
points: Probabilistic data structure with multiple layers of linked lists. Layer 0 has all elements; higher layers skip elements, mimicking binary search on linked lists! Achieves O(log n) average search time.
exam_tip: Mention that Skip List achieves binary search behavior on linked lists.

title: Self-Organizing Linked Lists: Move-to-Front Heuristic
points: Technique to optimize sequential search in linked lists. Move-to-Front: Whenever an element is accessed, move it to the head of the list. Exploit temporal locality for O(1) repeated access.
code:
// MTF Rule:
search(x) ==> remove(x); insertBeginning(x);
exam_tip: Self-organizing lists adapt to non-uniform access distributions.

title: Transpose Heuristic in Self-Organizing Lists
points: Whenever an element is accessed, swap it with its immediate predecessor (move forward by 1 position). More conservative than Move-to-Front; avoids erratic reorganization on single anomalous accesses.
code:
// Transpose Rule:
search(x) ==> swap(x->data, prev->data);
exam_tip: Contrast Move-to-Front (aggressive) with Transpose (gradual).

title: Unrolled Linked Lists: High Cache Locality
points: Hybrid structure: A linked list where each node contains an array of several elements rather than a single element. Combines O(1) linked list splitting with array CPU cache performance.
exam_tip: Unrolled lists dramatically reduce pointer memory overhead.

title: Memory Fragmentation Equation Proof
points: Heap with total free memory F = 800 KB, free holes: 200 KB, 150 KB, 250 KB, 200 KB. Largest hole M = 250 KB. Request = 300 KB. Prove request fails despite 800 KB free. Ext Frag = 1 - 250/800 = 68.75%.
code:
// Derivation:
Total Free F = 200 + 150 + 250 + 200 = 800 KB
Max Block M = 250 KB < 300 KB (FAILS)
External Frag E = 1 - (250 / 800) = 0.6875 (68.75%)
exam_tip: Write out the step-by-step subtraction clearly.

title: Circular Linked List Tail Insertion & Deletion Trace

title: Buddy System Memory Allocation Algorithm

title: Tree Terminology & Core Definitions
badge: KTU Part A • 3 Marks • Bloom's K1
points: Root: The unique top node with in-degree 0 (no parent).
Degree of a Node: The total number of subtrees (children) of that node.
Leaf (Terminal Node): A node with degree 0 (no children).
Internal (Non-Terminal): A node with at least one child (degree >= 1).
Height / Depth: Height of node is length of longest path to a leaf; Depth of node is length of path from root.
code:
// Tree Hierarchy Terms:
Root:      Level 0 (Depth 0)
Internal:  Degree >= 1
Leaf:      Degree == 0
Height:    Max Level in tree
exam_tip: Define at least 4 terms clearly to secure full 3 marks in Part A.

title: Binary Tree Types: Full, Complete, Perfect, Degenerate
badge: KTU Part A • 3 Marks • Bloom's K2
points: Full (Strictly) Binary Tree: Every node has either exactly 0 or 2 children (no node has degree 1).
Complete Binary Tree: All levels are completely filled except possibly the last, which is filled from left to right (Array representation friendly).
Perfect Binary Tree: All internal nodes have 2 children and all leaves are at the exact same level (Total nodes = 2^(h+1) - 1).
Degenerate (Skewed) Tree: Every internal node has only one child; performance degrades to a linear linked list O(n).
code:
// Visual Characteristics:
Full:       Nodes have 0 or 2 children
Complete:   Filled left-to-right at last level
Perfect:    Triangular symmetry (2^(h+1) - 1 nodes)
Skewed:     Left-skewed or Right-skewed chain
exam_tip: Differentiate strictly between 'Full' and 'Complete' binary trees!

title: Mathematical Properties of Binary Trees
points: Property 1: Maximum nodes at level i = 2^i (Root is level 0).
Property 2: Maximum nodes in a binary tree of height h = 2^(h+1) - 1.
Property 3: Minimum height of a binary tree with n nodes = floor(log2(n)).
Property 4 (Leaf vs Degree-2): In ANY non-empty binary tree, n0 = n2 + 1 (Number of leaves = Degree-2 nodes + 1).
Proof: Total edges E = n - 1. Also E = 1*n1 + 2*n2. Total nodes n = n0 + n1 + n2. Equating: n0 + n1 + n2 - 1 = n1 + 2n2 ==> n0 = n2 + 1.
code:
// The n0 = n2 + 1 Proof:
Total Edges: E = n - 1
Sum of Degrees: E = n1 + 2*n2
Since n = n0 + n1 + n2:
(n0 + n1 + n2) - 1 = n1 + 2*n2
==> n0 = n2 + 1 (Q.E.D.)
exam_tip: The n0 = n2 + 1 proof is asked in Part A and Part B regularly in KTU!

title: Binary Tree Representation: Array vs Linked
badge: KTU Part A • 3 Marks • Bloom's K2
points: Sequential (Array) Representation: Stores nodes in flat array using 1-based indexing. Parent(i) = floor(i/2), Left(i) = 2i, Right(i) = 2i+1. Excellent for complete trees; terribly wasteful for skewed trees (sparse array).
Linked Representation: Each node has data, left pointer, right pointer. Memory overhead: 2 pointers per node. Ideal for dynamic trees of arbitrary shapes.
Comparison: Array has O(1) parent/child calculation but fixed size; Linked has dynamic flexibility but 16-byte pointer overhead.
exam_tip: State the array index formulas: Parent = i/2, Left = 2i, Right = 2i+1.

title: Tree Traversals: Preorder, Inorder, Postorder (Recursive)
points: Preorder (Root -> Left -> Right): Visit root, traverse left subtree, traverse right subtree (Prefix notation).
Inorder (Left -> Root -> Right): Traverse left subtree, visit root, traverse right subtree (Infix notation; BST yields sorted order).
Postorder (Left -> Right -> Root): Traverse left subtree, traverse right subtree, visit root (Postfix notation; bottom-up deletion).
Time Complexity: O(n) for all three traversals (each node visited once). Space: O(h) call stack memory.
exam_tip: Write all 3 recursive functions; they are identical except for the print statement placement.

title: Iterative (Non-Recursive) Inorder Traversal using Stack
points: Algorithm: 1. Initialize empty stack S; 2. Initialize curr = root; 3. While curr != NULL or !isEmpty(S):
- Push curr and move left: `push(curr); curr = curr->left;`
- When curr is NULL: `curr = pop(); print(curr->data); curr = curr->right;`
Time Complexity: O(n) time. Space Complexity: O(h) auxiliary stack memory.
Eliminates Recursion Overhead: Preferred in production kernel and embedded systems.
exam_tip: State clearly why non-recursive traversal is preferred in stack-constrained hardware.

title: Level-Order Traversal (Breadth-First) using Queue
points: Principle: Visit nodes level by level from top to bottom, left to right. Requires a FIFO Queue.
Algorithm: 1. Enqueue root; 2. While queue not empty:
- `node = dequeue(); print(node->data);`
- `if (node->left) enqueue(node->left);`
- `if (node->right) enqueue(node->right);`
Time Complexity: O(n). Space Complexity: O(w) where w is maximum width of tree (up to n/2 at bottom level).
exam_tip: Level-order traversal uses a Queue, while Preorder/Inorder/Postorder use a Stack!

title: Tree Reconstruction: Inorder + Preorder
points: Given Traversals: Inorder: `D B E A F C` | Preorder: `A B D E C F`.
Step 1: First element of Preorder (`A`) is the ROOT of the tree.
Step 2: Find `A` in Inorder: `[D B E]` is Left Subtree, `[F C]` is Right Subtree.
Step 3: In Preorder, next 3 elements `[B D E]` correspond to left subtree (Root is `B`).
Step 4: Find `B` in `[D B E]`: `D` is left child, `E` is right child.
Step 5: Right subtree Preorder `[C F]`: Root is `C`. Inorder `[F C]` ==> `F` is left child of `C`.
Result: Root A -> Left B (Left D, Right E), Right C (Left F).
code:
// Reconstructed Tree Structure:
       A
     /   \
    B     C
   / \   /
  D   E F
Postorder: D E B F C A
exam_tip: Show the subtree splits at each recursive step to earn full methodology marks.

title: Tree Reconstruction: Inorder + Postorder
points: Given Traversals: Inorder: `4 2 5 1 6 3` | Postorder: `4 5 2 6 3 1`.
Step 1: Last element of Postorder (`1`) is the ROOT of the tree.
Step 2: Find `1` in Inorder: Left Subtree is `[4 2 5]`, Right Subtree is `[6 3]`.
Step 3: In Postorder, left elements `[4 5 2]` have root `2`. Inorder `[4 2 5]` ==> Left 4, Right 5.
Step 4: In Postorder, right elements `[6 3]` have root `3`. Inorder `[6 3]` ==> Left 6, Right NULL.
Result: Root 1 -> Left 2 (Left 4, Right 5), Right 3 (Left 6).
code:
// Reconstructed Tree:
       1
     /   \
    2     3
   / \   /
  4   5 6
Preorder: 1 2 4 5 3 6
exam_tip: In Postorder, the root is always the LAST element (rightmost).

title: Why Preorder + Postorder Cannot Uniquely Reconstruct Binary Tree
points: Ambiguity occurs when a node has only one child: Cannot determine whether child is Left or Right child without Inorder. Example: Preorder: A B, Postorder: B A could be B as left child OR right child.
code:
// Ambiguity:
Tree 1: A -> Left B
Tree 2: A -> Right B
Both have Preorder: A B and Postorder: B A!
exam_tip: State that Inorder traversal is mandatory because it specifies left vs right partition.

title: Expression Trees: Definition & Construction from Postfix
points: Leaves are operands; Internal nodes are operators. Algorithm: Scan postfix expression. Operands -> Create single-node tree, push pointer to stack. Operators -> Pop right child, pop left child, make operator root, push back.
exam_tip: First pop is RIGHT child; second pop is LEFT child!

title: Expression Tree Worked Example: `a b + c d e + * *`
points: Trace building expression tree from postfix `a b + c d e + * *`. 1. Stack: [a, b]; 2. `+` -> tree(a+b); 3. Stack: [(a+b), c, d, e]; 4. `+` -> (d+e); 5. `*` -> (c * (d+e)); 6. `*` -> ((a+b) * (c * (d+e))).
exam_tip: Draw the full expression tree with circled operator and operand nodes.

title: Threaded Binary Trees: Concept & Motivation
points: In a binary tree of n nodes, n+1 NULL pointers exist (wasting 50%+ pointer memory). Threaded trees replace NULL pointers with threads pointing to Inorder Predecessor (left) or Inorder Successor (right). Eliminates stack in traversal!
exam_tip: Explain that threads enable stack-free linear inorder traversal.

title: Binary Search Tree (BST) Definition & The Inorder Property
points: BST Property: For any node X, all keys in left subtree < X.key, and all keys in right subtree > X.key. GOLDEN THEOREM: Inorder traversal of a BST yields elements in strictly ascending sorted order!
exam_tip: State the ascending sorted order property of BST inorder traversal.

title: BST Search Operation: Recursive & Iterative
points: Compare target key with current node: key == root.data ==> found; key < root.data ==> search left; key > root.data ==> search right. Time: O(h) where h is tree height (O(log n) balanced, O(n) skewed).
exam_tip: Iterative search avoids call stack overhead; state both time complexities.

title: Finding Minimum and Maximum Elements in BST
points: Minimum key is located at the leftmost node (keep moving left until curr->left == NULL). Maximum key is located at rightmost node (keep moving right until curr->right == NULL). O(h) time.
code:
int findMin(struct TreeNode* r) { while(r->left) r = r->left; return r->data; }
int findMax(struct TreeNode* r) { while(r->right) r = r->right; return r->data; }
exam_tip: Highlight that findMin and findMax do not require inspecting the entire tree.

title: BST Insertion Operation: Algorithm & Code
points: Traverse down tree until a NULL child pointer is found where the new key belongs. Create new node and link to parent. Duplicates are generally rejected or stored in a frequency counter. O(h) time.
exam_tip: Show that insertion always attaches new nodes as LEAF nodes!

title: BST Insertion Trace on Keys: 50, 30, 20, 40, 70, 60, 80

title: Inorder Predecessor and Inorder Successor in BST
points: Inorder Predecessor: The maximum key in the left subtree (largest value smaller than node). Inorder Successor: The minimum key in the right subtree (smallest value larger than node).
exam_tip: Successor finding is the core subroutine for BST 2-child deletion.

title: BST Deletion — Case 1: Deleting a Leaf Node
points: Node to delete has degree 0 (no children). Simply set parent's pointer to NULL and free the node. Example: deleting 20, 40, 60, or 80. O(h) time to locate + O(1) to splice out.
exam_tip: Case 1 is the simplest: parent link becomes NULL.

title: BST Deletion — Case 2: Deleting a Node with One Child
points: Node has exactly one non-empty child (left or right). Bypass the node by linking parent directly to the single child, then free the node. Similar to deleting node from linked list.
exam_tip: Show the pointer bypass in your tree diagram.

title: BST Deletion — Case 3: Deleting a Node with Two Children
points: Node has two children. Cannot simply bypass. Method: 1. Find Inorder Successor (minimum in right subtree); 2. Copy successor's key to target node; 3. Recursively delete the successor from right subtree (which is Case 1 or Case 2!).
exam_tip: Explain why the Inorder Successor is guaranteed to have AT MOST one child!

title: BST Worst-Case Degradation to O(n) & Skewed Trees
points: When keys are inserted in strictly sorted order (e.g., 10, 20, 30, 40, 50), every node attaches as right child. Tree becomes a degenerate right-skewed list. Height becomes n, search degrades to O(n). Solution: Self-balancing trees (AVL, Red-Black).
exam_tip: State that self-balancing trees guarantee O(log n) height.

title: Binary Heap Definition: Shape & Heap-Order Properties
points: 1. Shape Property: Must be a COMPLETE binary tree (all levels filled except last, filled left-to-right). 2. Heap-Order Property: Max-Heap: A[Parent(i)] >= A[i]; Min-Heap: A[Parent(i)] <= A[i].
exam_tip: List both the Shape Property and the Heap-Order Property.

title: Max-Heap vs Min-Heap Comparison
points: Max-Heap: Value of node <= parent; Root is maximum; Used in Heap Sort ascending. Min-Heap: Value of node >= parent; Root is minimum; Used in Priority Queues, Dijkstra, Prim's algorithms.
exam_tip: Contrast root values and typical algorithm applications.

title: Array Representation of Binary Heap
points: Because a heap is a complete binary tree, it is mapped into a flat array without storing any child/parent pointers! 1-based indexing: Parent(i) = i/2, Left(i) = 2i, Right(i) = 2i+1. 0-based: Parent = (i-1)/2, Left = 2i+1, Right = 2i+2.
exam_tip: Remember: Array representation has ZERO pointer memory overhead!

title: Max-Heapify (Sift-Down) Algorithm
points: Assumes left and right subtrees of node i are already valid max-heaps, but A[i] may violate heap property. Compare A[i] with left and right children. Swap with largest. Recursively heapify the affected child. O(log n) time.
exam_tip: State the precondition: Subtrees of i must already be valid heaps.

title: Building a Heap (Build-Max-Heap Algorithm)
points: Bottom-up approach: Leaves (nodes from floor(n/2)+1 to n) are trivially valid 1-element heaps. Start heapifying from the last non-leaf node i = floor(n/2) down to root 1. Running time: O(n) linear!
exam_tip: Crucial index: Loop begins at `n / 2` because all nodes after n/2 are leaves!

title: Build-Max-Heap Worked Trace on Array `[4, 1, 3, 2, 16, 9, 10, 14, 8, 7]`
points: Array of 10 elements. Last non-leaf is index 5. 1. Heapify i=5 (A[5]=16): valid; 2. i=4 (A[4]=2): largest is 14 -> swap A[4], A[8]; 3. i=3 (A[3]=3): largest is 10 -> swap A[3], A[7]; 4. i=2 (A[2]=1): largest is 16; 5. i=1 (A[1]=4): largest is 16 -> sift down. Result is valid Max-Heap!
exam_tip: Draw the binary tree at each of the 5 heapify steps.

title: Mathematical Proof: Build-Heap Time Complexity is O(n)
points: At height h, maximum nodes is ceil(n / 2^(h+1)). Heapify at height h takes O(h) time. Total Work = sum_{h=0}^{log n} ceil(n / 2^(h+1)) * O(h) = O(n * sum_{h=0}^inf h / 2^h). Since sum h/2^h = 2, Total Work = O(n * 2) = O(n).
exam_tip: Derive the sum S = 2 completely; examiners look for the S - S/2 subtraction.

title: Heap Insertion (`insert`) Algorithm
points: 1. Increment heap size `n++`; 2. Place new key at bottom `A[n] = key`; 3. Sift-Up (Percolate Up): Compare A[i] with A[Parent(i)]. If A[i] > A[Parent(i)], swap and move up to parent. Repeat until root or property satisfied. O(log n) time.
exam_tip: Insertion uses Sift-Up (upwards), while Heapify uses Sift-Down (downwards).

title: Heap Extract-Max Algorithm
points: 1. Root A[1] is maximum. Store `max = A[1]`; 2. Move last element to root: `A[1] = A[n]; n--`; 3. Call `maxHeapify(A, n, 1)` to restore heap property from root downwards. O(log n) time.
exam_tip: Show that replacing root with last element preserves the complete binary tree shape.

title: Priority Queue Implementation via Binary Heap
points: A Priority Queue stores key-value pairs where elements are dequeued in order of priority. Binary Heap provides O(log n) `insert`, O(log n) `extractMax`, O(1) `findMax`, O(log n) `increaseKey`. Much faster than array O(n).
code:
// Priority Queue Complexity:
Operation       Heap       Unsorted Array
insert          O(log n)   O(1)
extractMax      O(log n)   O(n)
peekMax         O(1)       O(n)
exam_tip: State the four core priority queue operations and their heap complexities.

title: d-ary Heaps & Binomial Heaps Overview
points: d-ary Heap: Each node has d children. Reduces height to log_d(n), speeding up insert/increaseKey, but slows down extractMax (requires d-1 comparisons). Binomial / Fibonacci Heaps support O(1) merge.
exam_tip: Useful in network routing (Fibonacci heap optimizes Dijkstra to O(V log V + E)).

title: Graph Definitions: Vertices, Edges & Terminology
points: Graph G = (V, E) where V is set of vertices, E is set of edges. Directed Graph (Digraph): Edges have direction (u, v). Undirected Graph: Edges are bidirectional (u, v) == (v, u). Weighted: Edges carry numerical costs.
exam_tip: Define both Directed and Undirected graphs with edge notation.

title: Degree of a Vertex: In-Degree and Out-Degree
points: Undirected: Degree is number of edges incident on vertex. Handshaking Lemma: sum(deg(v)) = 2|E|. Directed: In-Degree is number of edges entering vertex; Out-Degree is number of edges leaving vertex.
exam_tip: State Handshaking Lemma and prove that total degree sum is always even.

title: Graph Representation 1: Adjacency Matrix
points: 2D array A[V][V] where A[u][v] = 1 (or weight w) if edge (u,v) exists, else 0. Symmetric for undirected graphs (A = A^T). Space complexity: O(V^2). Edge existence lookup: O(1). Finding all neighbors: O(V).
exam_tip: Emphasize that Adjacency Matrix wastes memory for sparse graphs where E << V^2.

title: Graph Representation 2: Adjacency List
points: Array of V linked lists. Adj[u] stores linked list of all vertices adjacent to u. Space complexity: O(V + E) for directed, O(V + 2E) for undirected. Finding neighbors: O(deg(u)). Optimal for sparse graphs.
code:
// Adjacency List Structure:
Adj[0] -> 1 -> 3 -> NULL
Adj[1] -> 0 -> 2 -> NULL
Adj[2] -> 1 -> 3 -> NULL
Adj[3] -> 0 -> 2 -> NULL
exam_tip: Highlight that Adjacency List is optimal when graph is sparse (E << V^2).

title: Adjacency Matrix vs Adjacency List Comparison Table
points: Space: Matrix O(V^2), List O(V + E). Edge Lookup (u,v): Matrix O(1), List O(deg(u)). Iterate Neighbors: Matrix O(V), List O(deg(u)). Add Edge: Matrix O(1), List O(1). Add Vertex: Matrix O(V^2) realloc, List O(1).
code:
// Master Graph Representation Table:
Operation           Adj Matrix    Adj List
Memory Space        O(V^2)        O(V + E)
Check edge (u, v)   O(1)          O(deg(u))
Iterate neighbors   O(V)          O(deg(u))
Best for            Dense graphs  Sparse graphs
exam_tip: Draw this 4-row comparison table for 3-mark representation questions.

title: Breadth-First Search (BFS) Principle & Algorithm
points: Explores graph level-by-level using a FIFO Queue and visited[] boolean array. 1. Enqueue source, visited[s]=true; 2. While queue not empty: u = dequeue(); for each unvisited neighbor v of u: visited[v]=true, enqueue(v). Time: O(V + E).
exam_tip: Mention that BFS finds the shortest path in unweighted graphs.

title: BFS Traversal Trace on 7-Vertex Graph
points: Given graph with vertices 0 to 6. Source 0. Show Queue contents and visited array at each step: Dequeue 0 -> Enqueue 1, 2. Dequeue 1 -> Enqueue 3, 4. Dequeue 2 -> Enqueue 5, 6. Traversal order: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
exam_tip: Construct the 4-column trace table with Queue contents at every step.

title: Depth-First Search (DFS) Principle & Algorithm
points: Explores graph along each branch as deeply as possible before backtracking. Implemented using Recursion or an explicit Stack. 1. visited[u] = true; print(u); 2. For each unvisited neighbor v of u: DFS(v). Time: O(V + E).
exam_tip: State both time complexity O(V + E) and call stack auxiliary space O(V).

title: DFS Traversal Trace on 7-Vertex Graph
points: Trace recursive DFS on graph from source 0. Show recursion call stack push and pop operations. Traversal order: 0 -> 1 -> 3 -> 4 -> 2 -> 5 -> 6. Contrast with BFS order.

// Call Stack Trace:
[DFS(3)]  <-- Top
[DFS(1)]
[DFS(0)]
Returns to 1, then branches to 4...
exam_tip: Draw the DFS discovery tree showing tree edges vs back edges.

title: Comparison: BFS vs DFS
points: Data Structure: BFS uses Queue (FIFO); DFS uses Stack (LIFO / Recursion). Traversal: BFS goes wide level-by-level; DFS goes deep along paths. Applications: BFS finds shortest path in unweighted graph; DFS detects cycles, finds connected components, topological sort.
